headwords.meaning: variant of Athow (see Athow)
at the lee, from residence thereby
headwords.author_comment: v. Lee; cf. Attwood and Attwell.

headwords.meaning: at the moor, from residence thereon
headwords.author_comment: v. Moor.

headwords.meaning: at the ridge, from residence thereby
headwords.author_comment: v. Rigg or Ridge; cf. Attwood or Attwell.

headwords.headword: Attwell, Atwell, Atwill, Attiwell, Attwill, Attewell
headwords.meaning: at the well, from residence thereby
headwords.author_comment: v. Wells; cf. Attwood. The variant Atwill is found as early as the beginning of the 17th century.

headwords.meaning: at the wood, from residence thereby
headwords.author_comment: cf. Attwell, and v. Wood. Every English county has representatives of this surname. Atwood has ramified strongly in Boston and the district.

headwords.meaning: the son of Adam, from the colloquial Addy
headwords.author_comment: Addy, q.v. This was sharpened into Atty. Similarly Addison became Attison.

headwords.meaning: at the water
headwords.author_comment: cf. Bywater, Attwood, Attwell, &c.; v. Waters. This surname, having crossed the Atlantic, is more strongly represented in New York than London.

headwords.meaning: at the wick
headwords.author_comment: v. Wick; cf. Attwood or Attwell. Still existing on authority of Lower (1860).

headwords.meaning: of Atworth; not a compound of 'atte' and 'worth', but from a parish in dioc. of Sarum
the son of Aubin; presumably a variant of Alban or Albin
headwords.author_comment: I presume a variant of Alban or Albin, q.v.; cf. St. Albyn for St. Alban.

headwords.meaning: the son of Aubrey (Domesday, Albericus); fem. Albreda, whence Aubrey, both masc. and fem.
the son of Aucher; see Auger
the son of Aldwin
headwords.author_comment: The ordinary and natural modification, v. Alden: cf. Bawden and other forms from Baldwin.

headwords.meaning: of Audley, a parish in dioc. Lichfield and co. Stafford, formerly Alditheley
headwords.author_comment: Aldith no doubt being the name of the original proprietor; v. Aldith.

headwords.meaning: see Awdry
the son of Aldus, a natural modification
headwords.author_comment: v. Aldhouse.

headwords.meaning: 'le Orfevre', the goldsmith
headwords.author_comment: v. Offer.

headwords.meaning: the son of Auger or Aucher, probably a French form of Oger, whence Odger
headwords.author_comment: Odger, q.v. Auger and Aucher are treated as the same name in the Visitation of Essex (1541), pp. 36, 181, 211, 753.

headwords.meaning: the son of Auguste
headwords.author_comment: Probably an importation from the Low Countries or France, as I find few traces of the name in England as a font-name, except in the form of Austin, q.v. The Boston (U.S.) Directory has August, Auguste, Augusta, Augustine, and Augustus among its list of surnames; cf. German August, Fr. Auguste.

headwords.meaning: the son of Augustine
headwords.author_comment: Popularly known in England as Austin, q.v. Augustine is a dim. of August, q.v.

headwords.meaning: the old, a North English form
headwords.author_comment: v. Ould; cf. Young, Yonge. The following is curious.

headwords.headword: Aust, Austen, Austin, Austing, Asten, Astin, Astins
headwords.meaning: the son of Augustine; O.E. Austin
headwords.author_comment: Very popular in the 13th century. 'Til he foundede freres of Austynes ordre': Piers Plowman, 10193-4. A whole column of Austin appears in the London Directory. The name was made common by the Austin Friars, or Black Canons, as they were often styled from their black cloaks, who were established early in the 12th century in England, and possessed of about 170 houses. Astin (q.v.), confounded often with the local Aston, was an early form.

headwords.meaning: the son of Auty (?); seemingly an early personal name
headwords.author_comment: Seemingly an early personal name. A well-known surname in co. York.

headwords.meaning: the son of Aveline; v. Eveline
headwords.author_comment: The g in Aveling is, of course, excrescent, as in Jennings. Aveline is found both in the 16th and 17th centuries as a font-name.

headwords.meaning: (?) the son of Avenel (?); origin queried by the author
headwords.author_comment: Always without prefix in the Hundred Rolls, whose instances are generally in the neighbourhood of co. Camb. Mr. Lower suggests a local origin from Avenelles, in the department of Eure. This is quite possible; one thing seems quite certain, the chief modern variant is Averill or Averell. Any one who has studied the corruptions undergone by surnames will feel no surprise at this.

headwords.meaning: the avener; O.F. avenier, avener, oat-merchant; a chief officer of the stable, who had charge of the provender for the horses (H.E.D.)
headwords.author_comment: 'The aveyner shall ordeyn provande good won / For the lordys horsis everychon.' 1460. Boke of Curtasye, 305. I am afraid the surname is extinct.

headwords.meaning: the son of Avery; v. Every
headwords.author_comment: Avery is strongly represented in the United States, especially in Boston. This is easily accounted for. Jacob Averie (aged 33) and George Averie (aged 23) sailed for Virginia in 1635. Others of the same name followed. (v. Hotten's Lists of Emigrants, p. 121, and v. Index.)

headwords.meaning: the son of Avis, originally Hawisia or Hawoyse
headwords.author_comment: This very soon settled into Avicia, Avice, or Avis. It was decidedly popular for several centuries, and is just coming into use again, after two hundred years of almost entire neglect. (For history of the name, v. Yonge, ii. 212.) For further instances, v. Haweis.

headwords.meaning: the son of Etheldreda, popularly Awdry
headwords.author_comment: St. Awdry's Fair is held on Oct. 17, at the Isle of Ely. Its St. Awdry necklaces, showy but cheap, gave rise to the term 'tawdry-lace,' whence adj. tawdry; v. Skeat.

headwords.meaning: of Awre, a parish in co. Glouc.
the son of ---- (?); origin uncertain, perhaps Atkinson
headwords.author_comment: This Lancashire and Cheshire surname has clearly no connexion with Axton (q.v.). It is a patronymic formed like Jaxon, Dixon, Dix, or Cox, which represent Jackson, Dickson, Dicks, or Cocks. I can but suggest that it is Atkinson, which in my part of Lancashire (Furness) is invariably pronounced Atkison or Akison; v. Atkinson.

headwords.meaning: (?) the son of Axell (?); probably a variant
of Axton, a hundred in co. Kent
headwords.author_comment: Axon in the south of England seems to be but a lazy corruption. The following entries (1557-77) manifestly refer to the same family.

headwords.meaning: the son of Aylwin, q.v.
headwords.author_comment: Compounds of win always corrupt to in, en, and ing; v. Golden and Golding for Goldwin. The g in Ayling is, of course, excrescent; cf. Jennings.
headwords.modern_distribution: MDB. (co. Essex), 1, 0, 1; London, 2, 11, 0; Boston (U.S.), 0, 1, 0; New York, 0, 2, 0

headwords.meaning: the son of Ailet
headwords.author_comment: This is the Domesday form of the personal name (Lower). For other forms, v. Allott.

headwords.meaning: the son of Ailof
headwords.author_comment: In Domesday.

headwords.meaning: the son of Aylmar or Ailmar
headwords.author_comment: Several instances occur in Domesday; v. Amery. A common surname in the Hundred Rolls. It was already going out of fashion in the 13th century as a font-name, and is rarely found as such in the 14th century, but it secured hereditary honours as a surname somewhat early, and as a consequence is well represented in our directories. The l is usually elided in the United States, but this occurred so early as the 13th century.

headwords.meaning: the son of Aylward; v. Allard
headwords.author_comment: This last variant (common in the Hundred Rolls) led on to Allard, q.v.

headwords.meaning: the son of Aylwin; v. Aylen
see Ainsley
the heir
headwords.author_comment: It is curious to note that while Ayre is the almost universal English form (saving Eyre), Ayer is equally universal in the United States. For early and other instances, v. Ayres and Eyre.

headwords.meaning: the son of the heir; a variant of Ayre or Eyre with the patronymic s suffixed
headwords.author_comment: No doubt a variant of Ayre or Eyre, q.v., with the patronymic s suffixed, as in Jones, Simmons, Roberts, &c. Therefore literally 'the son of the heir.' My first instance seems to set the matter at rest. Several families of Ayres or Aires went out to America in the 17th century, which fact accounts for its familiar recurrence in the United States; v. index, Hotten's Lists of Emigrants.

headwords.meaning: of Baylham, a parish two miles and a half from Needham, Market, co. Suffolk
headwords.author_comment: The surname is evidently imitative of Baalam.

headwords.meaning: the son of Barbara, from the nick. Babb
headwords.author_comment: Barbara was extremely popular in the 13th and 14th centuries; v. Barbot.

headwords.meaning: of Airton, a township in the parish of Kirkby-in-Malham-Sale, near Settle, West Rid. Yorks.
of Babbage
headwords.author_comment: Probably some local name with the same prefix as Babbacombe, co. Devon, from which district the family are sprung.
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 2, 2, 1; South Molton, co. Devon, 1, 0, 0; List of Farmers (Devonshire Dir.), 6, 0, 0; Boston (U.S.), 1, 5, 0

headwords.meaning: the son of Barbara; v. Barbot
of Baber
headwords.author_comment: Mr. Lower derives it from the Hundred of Babergh, co. Suffolk. But in the Cornwall Directory occurs a place called Baber, seemingly the same as St. Dominick. Baber is a familiar Devon and Cornwall surname.

headwords.meaning: variant of Ash and Ashford
headwords.author_comment: These seem to be Devonshire variants; cf. Ric. de Ayswell (Ashwell) or Philip de Ayston (Ashton), 1273. A (index).

headwords.meaning: of Babington, a parish in co. Somerset, five or six miles from Frome; also hamlets, Great and Little Babington, near Hexham, co. Northumberland
headwords.author_comment: The writer adds that branches of this family settled in cos. Derby and Leicester. From the latter Macaulay took his second name.

headwords.meaning: the bachelor; v. Batchelar and Batchelder
(1) at the back, i.e. one who resided in a cottage lying behind some others; (2) uncertain (printed '—— ?')
headwords.author_comment: In the Eastern Counties Back seems to correspond with the German Bache.

headwords.meaning: the baker, q.v.; cf. Backhouse and Baxter
headwords.author_comment: 'To . . . the backers wyffe, for v. mennes borde': 1466, Mann. and Househ. Exp. 211 (H.E.D.).

headwords.meaning: at the bake-house, from residence therein
headwords.author_comment: 'Bakehowse, or bakynge house: pistrina': Prompt. Parv. Halliwell mistakenly makes it a back-house, or wash-house (v. Backas, i. 130). 1502. Arnold, Chron. 93, 'Ye shal kepe noo bachous' (H.E.D.). With Bacchus (imitative), cf. Kirkus (Church-house), Malthus (Malt-house), or Loftus (Loft-house).
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 8, 0, 0; Crockford, 1, 0, 0; West Riding Court Dir., 8, 2, 0; Philadelphia, 0, 0, 9

headwords.meaning: the bachelor; v. Batchelor and Blackler
the bakester, a baker of bread, with the feminine suffix; originally a woman's occupation
headwords.author_comment: Langland speaks of 'Baksteres and brewesteres, And bochiers manye.' 'Baxter, bakstare, baker': Prompt. Parv. p. 21. Backster is one of the names in Foxe's list of Marian martyrs. The ordinances of the Guild of the Purification (Bishop's Lynn, 1367), are signed by 'Johannes Austyn, baxter' (English Guilds, p. 90). Capgrave says, 'In this same tyme (B.C. 205) lyved the eloquent man which hite (was called) Plautus, and for al his eloquens he was compelled for to dwell with a baxter, and grind his corne at a querne.'

headwords.meaning: the Bacon, a swineherd's sobriquet (?)
headwords.author_comment: A very common nick. in the Hundred Rolls; cf. Pigg, Wildbore, Hogg, affording proof that Bacon may have been used of a live pig originally.

headwords.meaning: the son of Adam; Welsh, Ap-Adam, equivalent to English Adamson
headwords.author_comment: cf. Bowen, Bevan, Bevans, Bethell, &c.

headwords.meaning: the son of Bartholomew, from nick. Bat or Bate, and suffix -cock
headwords.author_comment: v. Cock; cf. Wilcock, Jeffcock, &c.

headwords.meaning: of Baddiley, a parish in co. Chester, near Nantwich; also of Badley, a parish in co. Norfolk
headwords.author_comment: An unhappy corruption, of the imitative class, occurs in the following entry:-

headwords.meaning: the badger, a hawker, a dealer in corn and other commodities, buying in one place to sell in another
headwords.modern_distribution: Rotherham Dir., 4, 0; London, 7, 0; Crockford, 4, 0; West Rid. Court Dir., 7, 0; Boston (U.S.), 33, 0; New York, 3, 1

headwords.meaning: the son of Bartholomew, from nick. Bate or Bat, and dim. Batkin
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Wilkin, Watkin, &c.; v. Badcock.

headwords.meaning: see Bagnall
the son of Bagg
headwords.author_comment: This surname occurs frequently in early rolls, and always without prefix. There seems no reason to doubt its being a Scandinavian personal name. This is confirmed by the dim. Bagelyn (cf. Hewling) and by the entry Bagekoc, where the suffix -cock occurs, which is only added to font-names; v. Introd. p. 26. In this same record (Kirby's Quest) we find Bagshay, i.e. 'the hedged enclosure,' belonging to Bagg.

headwords.meaning: see Badger
(1) of Bagley (Bagley Wood is an extra-parochial liberty near Abingdon, co. Berks); (2) for a second parentage, see Baguley
of Bagnall, a chapelry in the parish of Stoke-upon-Trent, in the co. of Stafford
headwords.author_comment: Badnall is a modern corruption. Both forms are familiar in the county.

headwords.meaning: of Bagridge
headwords.author_comment: The Hundred Rolls mention a place called Baggeriggestrete, co. Dorset (A. i. 102).

headwords.meaning: of Bagshawe; probably 'the shaw of Bagg,' the first settler
headwords.author_comment: I cannot find the spot. Probably 'the shaw of Bagg,' the first settler; v. Bagg and Shaw.

headwords.meaning: the baxter; see Backster
of Baguley, a township near Northenden, co. Chester
headwords.author_comment: The Manchester Directory has Bagoley and Baggoley; v. Bagley.

headwords.headword: Bailey, Baillie, Bailly, Baily, Bayley, Baylie, Bayly, Baylis, Bayliss, Bayles, Bayless
headwords.meaning: the bailie, i.e. bailiff
headwords.author_comment: The same forms, or nearly all, may be seen in H.E.D. (v. Bailie); 'now obsolete in England, but retained in a special sense in Scotland'). O.F. bailli (13th cent.), later form of baillis (H.E.D.). Hence Baylis, Bayliss, &c.; cf. Jolly and Jolliffe. 'Artow than a bayely?' 'Ye,' quod he. -Chaucer, Freres Tale, 92 (quoted in H.E.D.).

headwords.meaning: of Bainbridge, a township in the parish of Aysgarth, N. Rid. Yorks
headwords.author_comment: This surname has spread widely, and ramified strongly.
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 11, 1, 1; West Riding Court Dir., 2, 0, 0; Philadelphia, 17, 0, 0

headwords.meaning: of Baines, some spot in co. York (?)
headwords.author_comment: Lower says 'a village near Bayeux in Normandy, probably so called from bain, a bath' (p. 16).
headwords.modern_distribution: West Riding Court Dir., 17, 3, 0; London, 17, 9, 0; Philadelphia, 7, 0, 10; New York (Baynes), 1

headwords.meaning: the baker; see Backster and Baxter
the balancer, a maker of balances or weighing machines
headwords.author_comment: 'Weighed in the balances,' Dan. v. 27. F. balance, 'a ballance, a pair of weights, or ballances,' Cotg. Cocke Lorelle's Bote includes- 'Aroweheders, maltermen, and cornemongers, Balancers, tynne-casters, and skryveners.'

headwords.meaning: (?) the son of Balch
headwords.author_comment: Mr. Lower suggests that this is an abbreviation of Balchin. I should rather say it was the parent; v. Balchin.

headwords.meaning: the son of Baldwin, from nick. Ball (q.v.) and suffix -kin
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Wilkin, Tompkin, &c. Balchin is a Dutch form. Lower says the fuller form Baldechin is a German surname. We may gather from the want of early instances that this is a name more recently introduced from the continent.

headwords.meaning: the son of Baldwin, from the nick. Ball (q.v.) with suffix -cock
headwords.author_comment: (v. Introd. p. 26); cf. Wilcock, &c. This has become corrupted to Bawcock, an ordinary corruption; cf. Shallcross and Shawcross. Still exists according to Lower.

headwords.meaning: equivalent to Ballard, q.v.
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Freebody, Goodbody, Handsomebody, or Peabody.

headwords.meaning: of Balderston, q.v.
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Kelson for Kelston. The suffix -ston is frequently modified to -son.

headwords.meaning: of Balderston or Balderstone, a parish in co. Lanc., near Blackburn
headwords.author_comment: V. Balderson.

headwords.meaning: of Baldock, a parish in co. Herts, eighteen miles from Hertford
the son of Baldric or Balderic
headwords.author_comment: V. Brodrick.

headwords.meaning: the son of Baldwin
headwords.author_comment: As a personal name, so popular in the surname period that it has left its mark deeply indented on all our modern directories; v. Ball, Bodden, Bawcock, &c. Baldwin occurs in Domesday. An aunt of the Conqueror married Baldwin, earl of Flanders; and William himself espoused Matilda, daughter of the fifth Baldwin of that earldom. No wonder Flanders was called 'Baldwin's land' (Freeman's Norm. Conq. i. 601).

headwords.meaning: the arbelister, an arbalester, or balister, a cross-bowman
headwords.author_comment: V. Banister and Alabaster.

headwords.meaning: 'the bulgy' or 'bulky', a stout, paunchy man
headwords.author_comment: V. Skeat (bulge and bulk); cf. Fatt, Bigg, Little, &c.

headwords.meaning: of Bakewell, a parish in co. Derby
(1) the son of Baldwin, from the nick. Bald, popularly Ball; (2) 'the bald'; (3) 'at the Ball,' a sign-name
headwords.author_comment: This was popularly Ball. The large number of Balls in the London Directory is accounted for by the great favour in which the name was held, and the constant influx from the Low Countries, where for a time it ruled supreme. The d in some cases might be dropped later on, on account of its suggesting baldness. We find Balcock in the Hundred Rolls, -cock being the suffix usually appended to the nick. of fontal names (v. Balcock). (2) v. Ballard. The representatives of this sobriquet have also dropped the final d to hide the truth. From either (1) or (2) or both came a pet name given to various animals. Ball is mentioned as the name of a horse in Chaucer and Tusser, of a sheep in the Promptorium, and of a dog in the Privy Purse Expenses of Henry VIII (Halliwell). 'Balle, schepys name': Prompt. Parv. p. 22. (3) cf. Bell, Roebuck, &c. This sign-name has existed for centuries.

headwords.meaning: 'bald-headed'
headwords.author_comment: The hair, or absence of it, gave us a large number of early nicknames, the majority of which still exist as surnames. Ballard seems to have been very popular for a bald-headed man; v. Ball. Professor Skeat quotes: 'And scorneden to hym saying, Stye up, ballard,' 1382: Wyclif, 2 Kings ii. 23.

headwords.meaning: 'le Balun,' i.e. the whale; Fr. baleine
variant of Bullinger
of Balne, a parish near Snaith, co. York
headwords.author_comment: The corruption was an early and natural one. The surname is well known in the county. The following entries occur in the same village (Wadworth).
headwords.modern_distribution: West Riding Court Dir., 1, 5; New York, 0, 2

headwords.meaning: of Balshaw, some spot in the vicinity of Lathom, co. Lanc.
of Bamber, now more familiarly known as Bamber Bridge, a village three miles from Preston, co. Lanc.
of Bambrough, a parish in co. Northumberland
of Bamfyld, some place in co. Devon or co. Somerset, whence in the latter Weston-Bamfyld, a parish six miles from Castle-Cary
headwords.author_comment: As a surname Banfield is the chief variant.
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 1, 1, 6, 0; Exeter (Banfill), 1; MDB. (co. Devon), 0, 1, 2, 0; Boston (U.S.), 0, 0, 5, 0; Philadelphia, 0, 1, 2, 0

headwords.meaning: of Bamford; Bircle-cum-Bamford is a township in the parish of Middleton, near Bury, co. Lanc.
headwords.author_comment: 'The estate of Bamford was granted to Thomas de Bamford by Sir Adam de Bury, temp. Henry III, for his homage and services,' &c.: Baines' Lanc. i. 525.

headwords.meaning: of Bampton, parishes in cos. Devon, Oxford, Cumberland, and Westm.
headwords.author_comment: A variant of the name is Banton, q.v.

headwords.meaning: of Banbury, a well-known town in co. Oxford
of the bank-croft, i.e. the enclosure on the slope
headwords.author_comment: An east Cheshire name that has many representatives in the directories of south-east Lancashire; v. Bank and Croft.

headwords.meaning: variant of Barnfather (v. Barnfather)
variant of Bamfield (v. Bamfield)
(1) a balister (l becoming n), an arbalester, a cross-bowman; (2) Local
headwords.author_comment: Cf. banisters, lit. balusters, staircase, railings. O.F. balestier: 'trecenti loricati, cum balistariis et artificibus machinarum multis' (Giles, i. 57, quoted by Freeman, Hist. Norm. Conq. iv. 583); v. Alabaster. The name in various forms is found in every early list. It is sufficient to turn to the London Directory to see by the number of Bannisters the commonness of the occupation. 'Gosners, balesters, and archers': Caxton, 1489 (quoted in H.E.D.). [Of John Corker, 1557:] Probably this is an instance of the curious Elizabethan custom of appending the old feminine -ster to names of masculine occupation. John Corker was, I suspect, the bailie or bailiff of the town. But he may have been a cross-bowman. [Of Adam de Banistre:] This is the only entry with de I can find. The Testa de Neville, Hundred Rolls, and Placita de Quo Warranto have many instances, but all without prefix. It is clear however that (1) is not the only origin, judging by the character of these entries. The surname is found all over the kingdom in large numbers. It is quite possible that some of these entries represent a personal name now forgotten.

headwords.meaning: 'at the bank,' i.e. the slope or declivity in the land
headwords.author_comment: Like all other local monosyllables, it takes a final s, perhaps the patronymic, as in Jones, Simmonds, &c.; cf. Brooks, Styles, &c.

headwords.meaning: variant of Bencher (v. Bencher)
'at the bank-knot,' one who resided on the knot or small prominence on the side of the bank
headwords.author_comment: The name looks anachronistic, and suggests the notes issued by the Bank of England.

headwords.meaning: variant of Bampton (v. Bampton, and cf. Banfield for Bamfield)
of Banwell, a parish in co. Somerset, near Axbridge
the son of Baptiste (French)
headwords.author_comment: I have not yet found Baptist as an English font-name before Henry VII. It never took root in England. The surname is very rare. Naturally, nearly all my instances are Johns.

headwords.meaning: the son of Barbara, from the nickname Barb, whence Babb, q.v.; a Norman-French form
headwords.author_comment: v. Yonge, i. 261.

headwords.meaning: the barber, one who trimmed or shaved beards
headwords.author_comment: v. Barbour.

headwords.meaning: the barberess, a female barber
headwords.author_comment: Matilda has long anticipated the lady barbers of to-day.

headwords.meaning: the son of Barbara, once popularly Barbery
headwords.author_comment: Barbara was a favourite font-name in the surname period; v. Babb, Barbot, &c.

headwords.meaning: at the barbican, from residence thereby; an outwork, an outwork of a fort
(1) of Barbon, a chapelry in the old parish of Kirkby Lonsdale; (2) of Barbourne, a parish in Worcestershire
headwords.author_comment: This originated Barbon and Barben, still existing in Furness and the district; v. Dalton in Furness Dir. To this place [Barbourne] we probably owe the south English Barbons, one of whom, Praise-god, was written variously Barbon, Barbone, and Barebones. A good deal of fun would have been lost to the world if a certain Parliament had been more correctly styled Barbon's Parliament. Even Barebones' Parliament is inaccurate, it should be Barebone's. 'The Long Parliament in Cromwell's time, called by derision the Rump, was headed by one Barebones, a leather-seller' (Curiosities of Literature). Here Isaac Disraeli is manifestly in error. Peck in his Desiderata Curiosa, speaking (1646) of a member of the family, styles him 'Mr. Barborne,' probably the original form, and suggesting Worcestershire as the home of the race.

headwords.meaning: the son of Barbara, nick. Barb or Bab, dims. Barbot and Babelot
headwords.author_comment: Diminutives in elot were not rare at the period; cf. Hamelot from Hamo, Richelot from Richard, and Hobelot or Robelot from Robert.

headwords.meaning: the barber; as a surname a North English form, and sometimes 'of Barbour' in Scotland
headwords.author_comment: 'A barbour was redi thare.' 1320, Sir Tristr. i. lxiii. (H.E.D.) 'She clepide the barbour': Wyclif, Judges xvi. 19.

headwords.meaning: a variant of Burchard
headwords.author_comment: v. Burchett.

headwords.meaning: of Berkeley (an early variant); Berkeley is a parish and market town in co. Gloucester
of Barcroft, a property in Cliviger, co. Lancashire
headwords.author_comment: A family of that name lived there until 1668, being found there so early as Hen. III; v. Baines' Lanc. (Croston's edit.), ii. 389. A rare surname in the 19th century—almost extinct, in fact.

headwords.meaning: the son of Bardolf
headwords.author_comment: (Yonge, ii. 404). 'Bardell: a corruption of Bardolf' (Lower). This statement is confirmed by the following entry: Osbertus Bardolf, alias Bardol, 45 Hen. III. BBB. p. 94. Cf. Randle or Randell for Randolph.

headwords.meaning: of Bardsley, a parish between Ashton and Oldham, near Manchester
headwords.author_comment: But some place in the south-west district must have borne the same name, judging from references given below. All the American Bardsleys, and all the North English Bardsleys, and perhaps all the Beardsleys, hail from the Lancashire parish stated above. The Ha above represents the now thriving parish of Hey, close to Oldham.
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 2, 0, 0; Manchester, 17, 1, 0; Ashton-under-Lyne, 3, 0, 0; New York, 3, 17, 2; Philadelphia, 24, 2, 1

headwords.meaning: of Bardwell, a parish in co. Suffolk, near Ixworth
variant of Barbon
on naked foot, one who went with feet bare; a friar or pilgrim
headwords.author_comment: 'Thy temple in Delphos wol I barefoot seke': Chaucer, The F. Tale, 11390. 'Fraunceys had his brethern Bar-fot to wenden.' Piers P. Creed, 593-4. 'A barefoote brother': Rom. and Jul. v. ii. 5.

headwords.meaning: at the Bargate; the entrance to a city, as Temple Bar
headwords.author_comment: Formed originally of posts and chain. 'The street, as well within as without the old Gate or Bar, called Fishergate Bar, goes by the name of Fishergate': Hist. and Ant. of York, 1785, ii. 189.

headwords.meaning: the barge-man
headwords.author_comment: The first entry below concerns three royal bargemen who attended the king in his journeys by water.

headwords.meaning: of Barham, a parish in co. Hunts, six miles from Kimbolton; also a parish in co. Kent, six miles from Canterbury; also a parish in co. Suffolk, four miles from Ipswich
the son of Baring
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Harding and Browning, q.v. 'The peer and the baronet descend from John Baring, of Devonshire, 18th century, son of John Baring, minister of the Lutheran church at Bremen, in Saxony' (Lower). Probably of the same parentage as Behring. True as the above may be, the same personal name was found on English soil in the surname period, and has its own descendants.

headwords.meaning: at the bark-house, where the bark was stored for tanning purposes; from residence therein or thereby
headwords.author_comment: v. Barker; cf. Bacchus, Malthus, Loftus, or Lewtas.

headwords.meaning: the barker, one who stripped trees of bark for the tanner; then a preparer of bark for tanning
headwords.author_comment: 'Escorceur, a barker of trees' (Cotg.). In the conversation between Edward IV and the tanner of Tamworth (Percy) it is said: 'What craftsman art thou?' said the king, 'I pray thee telle me trowe'; 'I am a barker, sir, by my trade; Now tell me, what art thou?' In the Chester Play the barkers and tanners marched together (Ormerod's Cheshire, i. 300).

headwords.meaning: local; the suffix being -ley, or -legh, or -legg, as in Whitelegg; spot unknown
headwords.author_comment: This curious-looking name is manifestly local, the suffix being -ley, or -legh, or -legg, as in Whitelegg, q.v. I do not know the spot.

headwords.meaning: (1) of Barlow (?), a probable variant; (2) of Barley, a parish in co. Herts, near Barkway
headwords.author_comment: No doubt (2) is the chief parent of our southern Barleys.

headwords.meaning: of Barlow, near Manchester
headwords.author_comment: The Lancashire Barlows spring from Barlow Hale and Barlow Moor, near Manchester. The name has ramified in an extraordinary manner. Barlow is also a parish in co. Derby, near Chesterfield, but nearly all our Barlows trace back to the neighbourhood of Manchester. The Barlows of Barlow Hale (whence William Barlow, bishop of Lincoln, born about 1550) were seated there so early as 20 Ric. II. The first entry below probably represents Barlow, a chapelry in the parish of Brayton, West Rid. Yorks.

headwords.meaning: of Barnby, q.v.

headwords.meaning: of Barnacle, a hamlet in the parish of Bulkington, six miles from Coventry, co. Warwick
the son of Bernard, or Barnard
headwords.author_comment: The Cistercian monk gave a wonderful impetus in the 13th century to this name, already popular. A large number of Bernards sprang up in Furness after the Abbey came under the Bernardine rule; Bernard Gilpin's name is a case in point. The popular form was Barnet. There are more than a hundred Barnetts in the London Directory. Barnes and Barnet seem to suggest a nick. Barn and a dim. Barnett. It is quite possible that such is the case, but in general Barnes must be looked on as local, and Barnett is simply a provincial pronunciation of Barnard. Barnet is turned into a title of high degree in the following entry: 'Of Barronet Coll, for his child's layreston, 1s. 8d.': Churchwardens' Accounts, Gateshead, 1643. For instances v. Bernard.

headwords.meaning: of Barnby, i.e. Barnby-upon-don, near Doncaster
headwords.author_comment: With Barmby, cf. Barnborough, or Barmborough, in same neighbourhood. Also cf. Bamfield and Banfield.
headwords.modern_distribution: West Rid. Court Dir., 1, 1; New York, 1, 0

headwords.meaning: (1) at the barn, from residence thereby; (2) the bairn, M.E. barne, a child

headwords.meaning: the bairn's father, father of the bairn or child
headwords.author_comment: v. Barne and Child; cf. Priestfather, q.v. The possessive s is unknown in these early North English entries.

headwords.meaning: the child's brother-in-law

headwords.author_comment: Barnwall is an American variant.

at the Bar, i.e. the entrance to the city or town, usually made of posts and chain

headwords.author_comment: Barrell is a modification, as the following entries show. (2) There seems to have been an early personal name Barel, which may share the parentage.

headwords.meaning: of Barry
headwords.author_comment: There can be little doubt that this was of Norman extraction; cf. the French Du Barry. The Irish Barrys have made a large inroad in the American directories. I cannot say whether they are of the same parentage or not.

the son of Barth, i.e. Bartholomew, from nick. Barth; v. Bate
the son of Bartholomew
headwords.author_comment: A great favourite in the surname period, as its nicks. and dims. (Bartle and Bartlett, q.v.) prove.

headwords.headword: Barthrop, Barthropp, Bartheropp, Bartropp, Bartrop, Bartrap

the son of Bartholomew, from the nick. Bartle, a form popular in north England
headwords.author_comment: For dim., v. Bartlett.

headwords.meaning: the son of Bartholomew; v. Bartlett

headwords.author_comment: A form of surname almost confined to Yorkshire, where Matthewman, Addyman, Priestman, and Vickerman (q.v.) arose.

headwords.meaning: the son of Bartholomew, from the nick. Bartle, and dim. Bartl-ot and Bartl-et
headwords.author_comment: I subjoin a few out of many instances in the Hundred Rolls. The variants were numerous. It is quite evident that Bartlet or Bartlot was the popular nick. for this then favourite Apostolic name.

headwords.meaning: (1) the son of Bartholomew, from the nick. Bartle and pet Bartl-ey; (2) of Berkeley, a variant
headwords.author_comment: cf. Charlie, Teddy, Bobbie, &c. Although looking strongly local, I find no evidence of this. We have, on the contrary, proof that Bartley owns Bartholomew as its parent. [Bartly Bradforth, co. York. W. 9.] This occurring in the county where Bartle was so popular clinches the argument; v. Bartle, Bartlett, Bate, &c. In the above two entries [under (2)] we see evidence that the west-country surname Berkeley was sometimes modified into Bartley.

headwords.meaning: (1) of the barton, literally the barley-croft; A.S. bere, barley, and tun, an enclosure; (2) of Barton
headwords.author_comment: Afterwards 'barton' got the secondary sense of a court-yard. (2) There are twenty-six parishes so called in Crockford. The origin is the same as (1), with this difference, that 'barton,' the single enclosure, had already grown into Barton, the hamlet or town.

headwords.author_comment: A small spot in Furness furnished a local surname which has spread. I could give many instances from the Ulverston register and the Lancashire Wills at Richmond, to which I simply refer the reader.

headwords.meaning: of Barwise
headwords.author_comment: I cannot find the spot. But although my earliest instance comes from co. Derby, I believe the parentage of the name will be found in Cumberland. Mr. Lower says, 'An ancient name at Ilekirk, co. Cumb.'

headwords.meaning: the base, i.e. of low stature; v. Bass

of Bascreville, 'now Bacqueville, in the arrondissement of Dieppe' (Lower)

headwords.author_comment: This is all I can suggest. But Lower says, 'Probably Fr. Basquet, a dim. of Basque, a native of Biscay; a page or footboy, because the natives of that province were often so employed.' If I am right, the change from P to B is, as is so common in nomenclature, imitative.

headwords.meaning: (1) probably of Baslow, a parish in co. Derby, three miles from Stoney Middleton; (2) of Bassaleg, a parish in co. Monmouth, near Newport (legge = lee; cf. Lee and Legh); (3) the son of Basil, from the pet Basily
headwords.author_comment: Let me put first the following entry: [Hugh fil. Basilie]. My other instances seem strongly confirmatory. I firmly believe (3) to be chief parent of the surname; cf. Charlie, Teddy, &c.; v. Bassil.

of low stature, short and stout, corresponding to the French 'le Bas'

headwords.author_comment: It is probable that most of the existing Bassetts can claim a local descent.

headwords.meaning: the son of Basil
headwords.author_comment: But more commonly a girl's name, in the form of Basilia or Basilie. It is now invariably a boy's name.

headwords.meaning: of Barnstaple, a parish in co. Devon; a manifest corruption; v. Barnstable
headwords.author_comment: The halfway to Bastable is seen in Barstaple. The following entry and note establish this derivation.

headwords.author_comment: A name proudly borne by at least one ancient English county family. 'William the Bastard' occurs in State documents as the Conqueror's surname.

headwords.meaning: the baster, probably a kitchen servitor who basted the joint
headwords.author_comment: 'Baster, one who bastes meat. 1525. Churchw. Acc. Heybridge (Nichols, 1797), p. 181, "To she that turned the spitt, 8d.: to the Basteter, 4d."' (H.E.D., v. Baster).

headwords.meaning: the son of Sebastian
headwords.author_comment: In early though rare use in Cornwall and south-west England, where Spanish influence would be expected to prevail. Popularly Bastian; cf. French Bastien, which perhaps had its effect on Basten. The form Bastion occurs in the Devonport Directory, co. Devon.

headwords.author_comment: Lower says, 'The keeper of a bath,' but without proof or reference. I look upon this as out of court; v. Batho.

headwords.meaning: Local (?); perhaps from a place-name with suffix -how (Bat-how); origin uncertain
headwords.author_comment: This surname, with its variants, has troubled me much. Cheshire seems to have been the home of the stock. It seems probable that the Shropshire Bathers represent another variant. If local, then, like Shillito, or Shillitoe, or Shafto, &c., the original suffix would be Bat-how (v. How). But this is all I dare suggest, as I can find no spot so entitled. Bathall again suggests a local Bathall, which would become popularly Bathaw.

headwords.meaning: (1) of Castle Bayard, near Grenoble; (2) the bay, a name of complexion, from bay, reddish brown, whence bayard, a bay horse
headwords.author_comment: Pierre Bayard, the knight sans peur et sans reproche, was born here in 1476. The English Bayard is, without doubt, a name of complexion; cf. Favel, a horse's name, and Burnel, an ass's name. 'As bold as is Bayard the blind,' i.e. a blind horse (Chaucer, C. T. 16881).

headwords.meaning: variant (corruption) of Baynham

headwords.meaning: the son of Barnard, q.v.

headwords.meaning: 'Ab-Eignon' (Welsh), i.e. the son of Eignon or Ennion
headwords.author_comment: A Gloucestershire surname. Robert ap Eignon had for his son Robert Baynham, of Chorewall, in the forest of Dean. Henceforward the family were so known (vide Visitation of Gloucestershire, 1623, p. 14; Harleian Soc.). The name looks wonderfully English and local, but, as shown, is not so. Beynon, Binyon, and Benyon, q.v., are other forms; but not Bunyan, I think.

headwords.meaning: of Beamish, a parish in co. Durham, seven miles from Gateshead

headwords.meaning: (1) Local, ---- ?; (2) the son of Benedict, from the nick. Ben, dim. Bennett
headwords.author_comment: On the same page as the preceding, in the same village, occurs Willelmus Benne. If the same, the origin is simple.

headwords.meaning: (?) at the bearblock (?), the block to which the bear was chained, from residence thereby
headwords.author_comment: Charles Bearblock occurs in the Devonport Directory, co. Devon, 1873.

headwords.meaning: the bearded
headwords.author_comment: An early surname. Speaking of Geoffrey Martel's death, A.D. 1060, Freeman says, 'To his namesake Geoffrey, surnamed the Bearded, he left Anjou and Saintogne' (Norm. Conqest, iii. 180); v. Withibeard.

variant of Bardsley
variant of Beer
the bearward, i.e. the keeper of a bear for exhibition of tricks; one who travels from place to place with a bear

headwords.meaning: the beater, a wool-beater, a fuller
headwords.author_comment: 'To full cloth is to felt the wool together: this is done by severe beating and pounding'; v. Full (3), (Skeat). 'Jacobus, the son of Joseph, was throwe there fro the pinacle of the temple, and after smet with a fuller's bat' (Capgrave's Chronicles, under date 30 A.D.; v. Woolbeater). 'A beter, verberator, baculator,' 1483 (Cath. Angl.).

headwords.meaning: the son of Beatrice, from nick. Bete and dim. Bet-on
headwords.author_comment: It is found till recent days in Cornwall, that last home of decayed forms of English font-names. But its origin does not appear to have been known. 'Beton the Brewestere Bade him good morrow.' Piers Plowman, Pass. V. 'Bete, or Betune, propyr name, Beatrix': Prompt. Parv. p. 34.

headwords.meaning: the son of Beatrice, nick. Bete; see Beaton
headwords.author_comment: Beatrice was, together with its nicks., a prime favourite in Yorkshire. The Poll Tax (1379) teems with it. Hence still largely represented; v. Beaton, Bettinson, and Betts. These two last entries agree with Prompt. Parv. supra; v. Beaton.

headwords.meaning: the son of Beatrice
headwords.author_comment: Beattie was the Northumbrian and Lowland Scotch form of the pet name. 'An abbreviation of the female name Beatrix' (Jamieson). The following variants of this surname are found on the Border: Baetie, Baitie, Baittie, Batie, Baty, Batye, Baytie, and Bette; v. The Debateable Land, by Robert Bruce Armstrong, p. 184.

headwords.meaning: of Beauchamp
headwords.author_comment: Mr. Lower mentions a Beauchamp near Avranches, and another near Havre. Its equivalent local term in England is Fairfield. Hugh de Bel-Champ, or Beauchamp (latinized in early records as 'de Bello-Campo'), obtained forty-three lordships from the Conqueror (Lower). Some of the variants may relate to some spot called Beecham (cf. Ashton), which would make them purely English, but I cannot find such a place.

headwords.meaning: 'the beauclerk' (a nickname of Henry I), 'learned clerk, good scholar'
headwords.author_comment: Cf. opposite characteristic in Mauclarke, q.v. 'Walker speaks satyrically of one who bribed a Bishop's secretary to pass him through his examination for orders, and so "rigged he returned to Wapenham a beauclerk"': Sufferings of the Clergy, edited by Whittaker, p. 176.

headwords.meaning: of Beau-Fai, in the arrondissement of Mortagne, in Normandy (Lower, p. 22)
'Beaufrere,' probably an address of courtesy like Beaupère, Bonamy, Belcher, and Bellamy; the exact equivalent of English 'Fairbrother'
headwords.author_comment: I doubt not buffer, a term of fellowship still in use, is thus explained. 'Well, old buffer,' was a common expression of greeting in my school-days.

headwords.headword: Beaumont, Beaman, Beament, Beamont, Beman, Bemand, Bement
headwords.meaning: de Belmont or de Beaumont
headwords.author_comment: 'Roger de Belmont appears in Domesday as a chief tenant in cos. Gloucester and Dorset' (Lower), probably a near kinsman of the Conqueror. 'The Itin. de la Normandie gives five places in that Province called Beaumont' (ibid.). Nearer home are parishes or places named Beaumont in cos. Cumb., Essex, and Leicester (ibid.). Generally speaking, the surname is of Norman extraction; v. Beaman.

headwords.meaning: of Beaupreau, a town in France
headwords.author_comment: Possibly its manufactures of linen and woollen originated the name of the linen fabric, beaupers or bewpers (v. H.E.D. 'beaupers'). At any rate, the fact that the surname existed and reached England is corroborative, as suggesting mercantile relations.

headwords.meaning: ab-Evan (Welsh), i.e. 'the son of Evan'
headwords.author_comment: v. Bevan and Bevans. Similarly Evan and Evans are found as Heaven and Heavens, q.v.

headwords.meaning: (1) 'de Beauver,' spelt in general history 'de Beauvoir'; (2) 'the beaver,' a sobriquet from the animal so called
headwords.author_comment: The Prior of Beauver is frequently alluded to in early registers.

headwords.meaning: (1) of Beauvais, in France; (2) a modification of Beavins or Bevins, q.v.
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Purkiss for Perkins.

headwords.meaning: the son of Barbara, a variant of Babb, q.v.
at the beck, from residence beside the beck, a running stream, a small rivulet
headwords.author_comment: A word still in common use in the North. 'Bek watyr, rendylle, rivulus, torrens': Prompt. Parv.

headwords.meaning: (?) the son of Becker (?); some old personal name
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Beckert (German) in London Directory.

headwords.meaning: (1) at the beck-head; v. A'Becket; (2) cf. Birkett; probably a personal name; cf. Becker
of Beckford, a parish in co. Gloucester, about six miles from Tewkesbury
of Beccles, a parish in co. Suffolk
of Beckley, (1) a parish in co. Oxford; (2) a parish in co. Sussex, near Rye
the son of Beckmann (German)
headwords.author_comment: For an English example, v. Bickman.

headwords.meaning: of Beckwith, a hamlet in the parish of Pannall, near Harrogate, co. York
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Askwith; no doubt the suffix is a variant of worth; v. Worth. This surname is strongly established in Boston (U.S.). 'Robert Beckwith, aged 21, went out in 1635 in the Transport, bound for Virginia' (v. Hotten's Lists of Emigrants, p. 103).
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 11; West Riding Court Dir., 5; Boston (U.S.), 10

headwords.meaning: of the bed; an official title: the yeoman of the bed-chamber
the beadle; v. Beadle

headwords.headword: Beddoe, Beddoes, Beddow, Bedow, Peddowe, Beddows
headwords.meaning: ap- or ab-Eddow, 'the son of Eddow' (a Welsh patronymic)
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Bevans, Bethell, Bloyd, Benyon, &c. My view is corroborated by the fact that Eddowe existed alongside Beddowe; cf. Bithell and Ithell, Ennion and Bennion. Also as Eddowe became Eddowes, so Beddoe became Beddoes; v. Eddowes. Although I may not have got the exact form of the personal name, there can be no doubt about the origin as stated above. Beddoes is a double patronymic, part English, part Welsh: ab-Eddow-s. This final s is the same as the s in Williams or Jennings; v. Bevans.

Radnor), 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0; (Salop), 2, 17, 3, 0, 0, 0; (Pembroke), 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0; (Montgomery), 0, 4, 0, 0, 0, 0; New York (Beddows), 1; Philadelphia, 1, 0, 3, 0, 0, 0

headwords.meaning: of Bedford, in the co. of Bedford
of Bedingham, parishes in diocs. of Norwich and Chichester
headwords.author_comment: It is possible that in some instances Beadman is a corrupted form. We have parallel instances in Deadman for Debenham, and Putman for Putnam, i.e. Puttenham. Of course it would be more satisfactory to refer it to the same origin as Paternoster, and there is strong evidence for this view. The corruptions would be as follows: Bedingham, Beddenham, Bednam, Bedman, Beadman; v. Beadman for a really satisfactory solution of that surname.

headwords.meaning: ab-Edward (Welsh) = English Edwards or Edwardson; v. Bellis for further instances
headwords.author_comment: Only found on the borders of the Principality. In the 18th century this had assumed the form of Bedward. From Bedward to Beddard was an easy and natural step. The above entry is very Welsh.

headwords.meaning: of Bedwin, two parishes, Great and Little Bedwin, in co. Wilts
(1) 'the bee,' an industrious man, a busy woman; (2) 'the son of Beatrice,' from the nick. Bee, still in use
of Beeby, a village six miles from Leicester; v. Bibby
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 2, 5, 0, 0; MDB. (co. Leicester), 0, 1, 0, 0; (co. Wilts), 0, 0, 2, 0; (co. Stafford), 0, 0, 0, 12; Philadelphia, 12, 0, 0, 0

headwords.meaning: at the beech-tree; cf. Ash, Oak, Birch, &c.
see Beauchamp
(1) 'le Becher' (avocation unknown); (2) 'the beecher,' one who lived by some prominent beech-tree (v. Beech); cf. Bridger
headwords.author_comment: I am not able to state the avocation followed by 'le Becher.'

headwords.meaning: at the Beech-ey, i.e. the beech-isle, the little island covered with beech-trees; or at the Beech-hey, the beech enclosure
headwords.author_comment: Seemingly some small islet in one of the streams or rivers in co. Oxford.—I wrote the above several years ago, but I find a second derivation, and possibly the true one in all cases: [Brownyng Bycheheye, co. Soms., 1 Edw. III: Kirby's Quest, p. 94.] This means Browning at the Beech-hey, i.e. he lived beside the beech enclosure; v. Hey, a field enclosed by beech-trees.

headwords.meaning: at the bere-croft, i.e. barley-croft (v. Croft); cf. Rycroft. A.S. bere, barley
headwords.author_comment: Evidently a Yorkshire local surname. I find no instances in the London church registers printed by the Harleian Society. There can be no doubt about the origin of this name.
headwords.modern_distribution: West Riding Court Dir., 4; London, 4; MDB. (West Riding Yorks), 5; Philadelphia, 9

headwords.meaning: 'the Beef,' beef, an ox; O.F. boef; cf. Bull, Pigg, &c.
a corruption of Beaumont; v. Beaman
at the bere, i.e. at the byre, the farmstead, cowshed, or village; v. Words and Places, p. 157; cf. Coneybeare
headwords.author_comment: Common in Devonshire place-names. The same as by in Formby, Rugby, Willoughby, &c.; cf. such places as Bere Ferrars, Bere Regis, Beer Alston, Beer Hacket, Langabeer, all in Devonshire and Dorset district.
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 12, 4, 1, 6; Plymouth, 4, 0, 2, 0; Exeter, 6, 0, 0, 0; Devonport, 4, 0, 0, 0; New York, 26, 3, 2, 15

headwords.meaning: the beer-brewer
headwords.author_comment: 'Chymney-sweepers, and costerdemongers, Lodemen and berebrewers.' Cocke Lorelle's Bote.

headwords.meaning: of Beeston, a village near Leeds
headwords.author_comment: With Beeson, cf. Kelson for Kelston, &c.
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 8, 0, 0; Sheffield, 1, 2, 0; West Riding Court Dir., 0, 2, 1; Philadelphia, 1, 2, 0

headwords.meaning: the son of Beatrice, from the nick. Bete; v. Beaton and Beatson
headwords.author_comment: Bete or Beet was a familiar nick. in Yorkshire, where Beatrice was very popular as a font-name in the 13th and 14th centuries.

headwords.meaning: see Beatson and Beet
'bel-sire,' grandfather, or perhaps bel chere, good friend; cf. Bellamy, Bowsher, and Bonamy
headwords.author_comment: 'Lo, here is the belschere broght that ye bad bring': York Mystery Plays, p. 262. 'Belsyre, or belfather, faders or moders fader, avus': Prompt. Parv. See also Belsire (H.E.D.).

headwords.meaning: 'handsome legs'; cf. Foljambe
(1) 'the son of Bell,' i.e. Isabel; nick. Bella or Bell; v. Belson; (2) 'le bel,' i.e. the beautiful; (3) 'at the Bell,' i.e. an inn-sign, or one who dwelt by the bell, i.e. bell-chamber
a familiar expression, 'my good friend'; cf. Bonamy
headwords.author_comment: A common surname in early registers. 'Feste! fy! that were a wykyd treson! Belamy, thou shal be smytt.' York Mystery Plays, p. 391. 'Thou bel-amy, thou pardoner,' he said. Chaucer, C. T. 12252. 'Belamy, fayre frynde': Prompt. Parv. p. 29.

headwords.meaning: see Bellhird
of Belencombre, in the arrondissement of Dieppe, in Normandy
headwords.author_comment: The present forms are imitative. There is not the slightest evidence in favour of an origin akin to Bellhouse. Dr. Charnock has unwisely permitted himself to write as follows: 'A friend assures me he knows of a William Chambers who changed his name to Bill-chambers, of which he says Bellchambers is a corruption' (Ludus Patronymicus, p. 6). 'Save me from my friends' receives a fresh consecration after this.

headwords.meaning: (?) 'the son of Isabel' (?), from the nick. Bel, dim. Bel-ot or Bel-et; v. Bell (1)
headwords.author_comment: The writer of the article on Hugh Bellot (1542-96), bishop of Chester (Dict. Nat. Biog. iv. 195), says, 'The Bellots were early seated in Norfolk. ... It has been suggested that the name is derived from belette, a weasel, or belotte, gentle, pretty. ... We find the name spelt in various ways: Billet, Bellott, Billett, &c.' After writing the above I find a local origin implied by two entries in Blomefield's Hist. of Norfolk. If correct, those entries are entitled to the first consideration. But I strongly suspect a double origin.

headwords.meaning: 'a bull-herd,' a tender of bulls; A.S. bellan, to bellow; cf. Coward, Oxhird, Calvert, Stoddart, or Shepherd
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Coward, Oxhird, Calvert, Stoddart, or Shepherd.

headwords.meaning: at the Bell-house
headwords.author_comment: The bell-house or tower was frequently detached from the church; v. Bell-house (H.E.D.), early corrupted to Bellows.

headwords.meaning: (1) the son of Beranger, a corruption, v. Berringer; (2) v. Bullinger
headwords.author_comment: The first is the more probable origin.

headwords.meaning: (1) of Bellingham, a parish in co. Northumberland; (2) of Billingham, a parish in co. Durham
headwords.author_comment: I strongly suspect that some small spot, also called Bellingham, existed or exists in co. Norfolk, whence some of our Bellinghams and Billinghams. Mr. Lower says there is a family of Bellinghams in co. Sussex, sprung 'from Belingeham, a manor near Hastings, mentioned in Domesday' (Patr. Brit. p. 24).

headwords.meaning: the son of Enion; Welsh Ap-Enion = Bennion, q.v.; further corrupted to Bellion
headwords.author_comment: Cf. banisters for balusters, staircase railings; n and l are constantly interchangeable in nomenclature.

headwords.meaning: the son of Ellis, from Welsh Ap-Ellis, which became Bellis
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Bloyd = Ap-Lloyd, Bethell = Ap-Ithell, Beddard = Ap-Edward. Found much in Cheshire and the borders of the Principality. Also in cos. Denbigh and Flint.
headwords.modern_distribution: MDB. (co. Ches.), 1, 0, 1, 4; Liverpool, 6, 0, 0, 0; March, 2, 0, 0, 0; London, 0, 1, 0, 0; Philadelphia, 8, 0, 0, 0

headwords.meaning: the son of Bell; v. Bell (1) and Belson
headwords.author_comment: The i in Bellison either represents the a in Bella-son, or is euphonically intrusive, as the a in Greenaway (for Greenway) or Ottaway (for Otway).

headwords.meaning: a bell-ringer (cf. Knowler), probably the old town-crier, or the officer who rang the hours in corporate towns
headwords.author_comment: The first two following entries seem to suggest a second derivation.

headwords.meaning: the bell-wether
headwords.author_comment: 'A very early instance of the use of this word will be found in the custumal of the manor of Brithwolton, co. Berks (Camden Soc.), where the keeper of the wethers was entitled, among his perquisites, to the belwether's fleece ("belwertheresfles"). The date is 1284-5.' (J. H. Round in Notes and Queries, Feb. 19, 1887.)

headwords.meaning: of Belchamp, a parish in co. Essex, three miles from Clare
of Belshaw or Balshaw
headwords.author_comment: I cannot identify the spot.

headwords.meaning: the son of Bell, i.e. Isabel; v. Bell (1)
of Belstead, a parish in the dioc. of Norwich and co. Suffolk
headwords.author_comment: This surname is in general lost in Benstead, q.v.

headwords.meaning: a bell-founder; v. Billiter
of Belton, parishes in diocs. of Norwich, Lincoln, and Peterborough
headwords.author_comment: The Lincoln Beltons have strongly ramified in that county.

headwords.meaning: (1) a bee-man, a 'custos avium'; (2) a corruption of Beaumont; v. Beaman
headwords.author_comment: For want of proof in favour of (1) it is manifest that (2) is the chief parent. The occurrence of Beaman in Yorkshire is strongly corroborative.

headwords.meaning: v. Beman, Beaman, and Beaumont
of Bembridge, a chapelry in the parish of Brading, Isle of Wight
headwords.author_comment: Sometimes probably a variant of Bainbridge, q.v. The following entries will show the tendency to variation. These, no doubt, were all related to one another.

headwords.meaning: 'Bendbow,' a complimentary sobriquet for a stout archer
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Stiffbow, Strongbow, Sharparrow, &c. 'Let the archer bend his bow.'—Jer. li. 3 (Auth. Version).

headwords.meaning: the son of Bennett
headwords.author_comment: v. Benns; cf. Evance for Evans.

headwords.meaning: the bencher, the banker
headwords.author_comment: Very early instances of some office in legal or exchequer matters, although the instances given in the H.E.D. belong to the 16th century.

headwords.meaning: the son of Benedict, more generally Bennet, q.v.
headwords.author_comment: One of the most popular personal names of the surname epoch, owing its favour to the Benedictines. Several of its derivatives, such as Bennet, Bennett, and Benson, are among the most familiar of English surnames.

headwords.meaning: uncertain (printed '?—')
the son of Benjamin
headwords.author_comment: Most of the instances in the London Directory are modern Jewish, but several, no doubt, represent a period when Benjamin, like Joseph, was not unpopular in England.

headwords.meaning: the son of Bennet, i.e. Benedict, from the nick. Benn
headwords.author_comment: It has nothing to do with Benjamin. Benn is a familiar surname wherever the Benedictine monks had a convent. Furness Abbey, founded in the 12th century, has made Benn and Benson (q.v.) a common surname in Furness and south Cumberland.

headwords.meaning: the son of Bennet, i.e. Benedict, q.v.
headwords.author_comment: Bennet was the usual English form. While Furness Abbey was administrated under the Benedictine Order, Bennet was one of the commonest of baptismal names in the surrounding district (v. Benn). West, in his Hist. of Furness (pp. 188, 60, 29), records, amongst the benefactors of the Abbey and Conishead Priory, 'Benet, son of Alan,' 'Benet Penington' (1290), 'Benet de Rotington' (1256), and 'Benet, son of William' (1256). These were all living in the immediate neighbourhood of the Abbey. Indeed, it will be found that Bennet and Benson are still common surnames in districts where the Benedictines have had foundations. The feminine Benedicta was also familiarly Bennet.

headwords.meaning: the son of Bennet, i.e. Benedict, from the nick. Benn, colloquially Benny or Bennie
headwords.author_comment: As a surname very rare; v. Benn and Benson.

headwords.meaning: the son of Benning
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Harding, Browning, &c. Among our place-names we have Bennington, Benningbrough, and Benningholme.

headwords.meaning: of Bennington, two parishes in co. Linc., one near Boston, the other seven miles from Grantham
Welsh Ap-Enion (the son of Enion); v. Benyon
the son of Bennet, i.e. Benedict; v. Bennet
headwords.author_comment: This surname in south Lancashire was at first Bennetson, but naturally settled down into Bennison. Later on this form disappears, and Bennison takes its place. Thus Bennison is not an extension of Benson, although the ultimate origin is the same, but an abbreviation of Bennetson.

headwords.meaning: the son of Bennet, from the nick. Benn; v. Benson and Benn
headwords.author_comment: The patronymic Bens became Bence; cf. Ellice for Ellis, Evance for Evans. And as regards the patronymic s, cf. Jones, Williams, Richards, &c.
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 1, 0, 0; MDB. (co. Norfolk), 5, 1, 0; New York, 0, 1, 0; Boston (U.S.), 0, 0, 4

headwords.meaning: the son of Bennet, i.e. Benedict, from the nick. Ben or Benn
headwords.author_comment: This great Benedictine name has made its mark on the modern directory in several surnames, but after Bennet, Benson occupies the first place.
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 28; MDB. (West Rid. Yorks), 10; Manchester, 10; Philadelphia, 74

headwords.meaning: of Binstead or Binsted, parishes in cos. Sussex and Hants
at the Bend or Bent, from residence thereby
headwords.author_comment: Probably the bend in a river, or valley, or hillside.

headwords.meaning: of Benthall, a parish in co. Salop, near Much Wenlock
of Bentham, a parish in West Rid. Yorks, twelve miles from Settle
headwords.author_comment: Most of the Benthams in the Dict. Nat. Biog. are referred back to a Yorkshire parentage. [Of the three 1379 entries:] All three were inhabitants of Bentham.
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 2; West Riding Court Dir., 3; Boston (U.S.), 2

headwords.meaning: of Bentley, parishes in cos. Suffolk, Hants, Warwick, Derby, and Essex; also many small hamlets in various counties
headwords.author_comment: In general the surname is literally Benet-legh, i.e. 'the field of Benedict,' the first occupier; v. Bennet.
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 29; West Riding Court Dir., 24; New York, 25

headwords.meaning: of Benwell, a township in the parish of St. John, Newcastle-on-Tyne
Ap-Eignion, or Eignon, or Enion, i.e. 'the son of Eignion,' &c.
headwords.author_comment: A once popular name in the Principality. St. Einiawn was one of the early saints of the Cymry, after whom is named a spring at Llanvareth, in Radnorshire (Yonge, ii. 161); v. Eynon and Baynham, and cf. Bevan for Ap-Evan, Bowen for Ap-Owen.

headwords.meaning: of Beresford, a manor and township in Astonfield, co. Stafford
headwords.author_comment: Possessed by the ancestors of the several noble families of this name (Lower, Patr. Brit. p. 26).

headwords.meaning: a shepherd; Fr. berger
headwords.author_comment: 'Bercaria or Berceria (Old Law), a sheep-pen, or sheep-fold' (Bailey's Dict. 1742). 'Bergeret, a pastoral song' (Chaucer). A statute, 37 Edw. III, c. 14 (1363), speaks of 'bovers, vachers, berchers, porchers, &c.' (v. full quotation under 'Day').

headwords.meaning: variant of Berryman
variant of Barclay
the son of Bernard, dim. Bernard-in; v. Barnard
the Berner (cf. Ventrer), one who had charge of fresh relays of dogs in hunting, a huntsman; O.F. brenier, bernier, berner
headwords.author_comment: Godefroy, i. 727 A). Notes and Queries, p. 370, 1885). Special mention of the 'berner' is made in a hunting record, 5 Hen. III (Rot. Litt. Claus. i. 462; N. and Q. above). The 'yeoman-berner' is mentioned in the Parliamentary Rolls. For a full account of this word and name, v. H.E.D.

headwords.meaning: of Berney, a town in the hundred of North Greenhow, co. Norf.
of Burghill, a parish in co. Hereford, four miles from Hereford
headwords.author_comment: This probably is also the source of the references to cos. Soms. and Devon. Of the others I can say nothing, because I cannot identify the spot.

headwords.meaning: see Barrat
the berrier, i.e. the thresher
headwords.author_comment: 'Berrier, a thrasher, North.' 'Berry, to thrash corn, North.' (Halliwell.) 'iij plewmen, j berryer, and j hird,' 1573: Wills and Inv. N. C. 399 (H.E.D.).

headwords.meaning: the son of Berenger
headwords.author_comment: Barengaria was a fem. form familiar to English history. French, Béranger; Germ. Berangar; Span. Berenger (Yonge, ii. 275).

headwords.meaning: at the Bury, i.e. borough; v. Bury, Burrows, Burroughes, &c.
headwords.author_comment: The Yorkshire folk have a strong propensity for quaint and humorous baptismal names. Father and son are thus described in the West Riding Directory (Stainland): John Berry, shopkeeper; Young John Berry, clogger. Young John was the son's fontal name.

headwords.meaning: (1) the bury-man, i.e. borough-man, a man dwelling within the borough; v. Berry; (2) possibly official, from the bearer of the name occupying some position akin to a borough-reeve
headwords.author_comment: As a rule a West-country name.

headwords.meaning: see Birkinshaw
the son of Bertin
headwords.author_comment: St. Bertin of France made the font-name familiar in that country, and as a French surname it occurs in the Lon. Dir. We must ascribe the English surname to the same source, although there seems strong evidence in favour of its being a pet form of Bertram, nick. Bert, dim. Bert-in. The early Bertie was evidently a popular form of Bertin. Bertram and Bertin are probably one and the same individual. Compare this also with Bertyn Flecchar, above recorded, same date.

headwords.meaning: the son of Bertram; v. Bartram and Bertin
of Berwick-on-Tweed; but v. Barwick
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Derby and Darby, or Clerke and Clarke, or Perkins and Parkins.

headwords.headword: Besant, Bezant, Bessant, Beasant, Bes[z]ant?, Beaza[nt]?, Bayzand
headwords.meaning: of Byzantium (?), i.e. an immigrant from Byzantium; or possibly from the coin, the bezant
headwords.author_comment: 'To oone he gave fyve [...] or besauntis,' 1382, Wyclif [...] xxv. 15); v. H.E.D. for va[rious] instances. 'A bisaunt, bezant, [...] bizantine was an old coin both in gold and silver, and so called from having been minted at Byzantium. The silver bezant passed current for 2s. or thereabouts' (Pipe Rolls, vol. iii. p. 74: Pipe Roll Soc.). As almost every other coin has its representative in our nomenclature so may this. More probably, however, like Turk and Saracen, it is local, denoting an immigrant from Byzantium. [Headword and etymology printed on p. 97, where part of the headword and commentary is covered by a folded flap of paper in the scan.]
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 3, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 0; MDB. (co. Glouc.) Bayzand, 1; New York, 3, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0

headwords.meaning: the beast, probably not in an uncomplimentary sense; M.E. beste or best
headwords.author_comment: Cf. beast in the Authorized Version of the Bible, especially in the Book of the Revelation; cf. Bull, Stott, Bullock, &c. 'Neyther man ne best.' Chaucer, C. T. 1978.
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 30, 0; West Riding Court Dir., 11, 0; Philadelphia, 34, 1

headwords.meaning: (1) of Beswick, lately a small hamlet one mile and a half from Manchester, now a suburb of that city; (2) of Beswick, a township in the parish of Kilnwick, East Riding of Yorkshire
headwords.author_comment: The many Beswicks of Lancashire undoubtedly hail from (1).

headwords.meaning: of Beetham, a parish in co. Westm., near Burton-in-Kendal
Welsh, Ap-Ithell, 'the son of Ithell'; cf. Bevan, Bloyd, &c.
headwords.author_comment: Lewlyn ap Ithel, 1325. M; Evan ap Ithell. Z; Jevan ap Ithell. Z; Ann Ithell. HH; Ithell Wynn. AA. 1. Bethell is still a considerable surname in the Principality. John Bithell is found among the List of Freemen in Chester, 1747.

headwords.meaning: of Bethune, in Artois
headwords.author_comment: Of course Beaton has a baptismal origin also; v. Beaton. But the Scotch Beatons, of whom came the great cardinal, are probably Bethunes. The Testa de Neville mentions the 'Advocatus de Bethun,' alias 'Betun,' alias 'Beton' (pp. 32, 36, 279).

headwords.meaning: the son of Beatrice, from the nick. Bete, dim. Beton; v. Beaton
the son of Beatrice, from the nick. Bete or Bet; v. Beaton and Beatson
headwords.author_comment: No connexion with Elizabeth. Both the nick. and the dim. occur together in Piers Plowman: 'And bade Bette cut a bough, And beat Betoun therewith.' Pass V.

headwords.meaning: the son of Beatrice, from the nick. Bet or Bett, and pet Bettie; cf. Charley or Teddie
headwords.author_comment: No connexion with Elizabeth; v. Betis.

headwords.meaning: 'Ab-Evan' ('the son of Evan') = Bevan (Welsh)
headwords.author_comment: The d in Bevand is excrescent, as in Simmonds. Howel ap-Evan, c. 1300. M; Eygneun ap Yevan. D. John and Richard Bevand are contained in the List of Freemen in Chester, 1747. Bevans is a double patronymic, part English, part Welsh = ab-Evan-s; v. Beddoes.

headwords.meaning: see Beaver
the son of Beverache; probably a personal name
headwords.author_comment: Like Aldridge (from personal name Aldrich), Beveridge has a distinctly local look about it. But the instances below make the question very doubtful. If a nick., v. Beverage (H.E.D.). Probably a personal name.

headwords.meaning: of Beverley, a town in the East Riding of Yorkshire
of Bavington; Great and Little Bavington are townships in the parish of Bellingham, co. Northumberland
of Bewick; Old and New Bewick, places in co. Northumberland
headwords.author_comment: A surname still familiar on the English border. Thomas Bewick, the wood engraver, was born in the parish of Ovingham in Northumberland.

headwords.meaning: see Bowsher
the beyer (?); perhaps a 'buyer,' one who purchased for the household
headwords.author_comment: One instance in the London Directory, at least, is foreign.

headwords.meaning: 'Ab-Enion'; Welsh, 'the son of Enion'
headwords.author_comment: One of many existing forms; v. Baynham, Bennion, and Benyon. Two of the four clergymen in Crockford hold Welsh livings. Enion seems to have been the William or John of the Principality in the surname period.
headwords.modern_distribution: Crockford, 4, 0; London, 5, 0; Liverpool, 2, 1; MDB. (co. Glamorgan), 8, 0; (co. Carmarthen), 9, 0; Philadelphia, 1, 1

headwords.meaning: the son of Bibby, i.e. Isabella
headwords.author_comment: There can be little doubt about this derivation. Bibby is a York and Lancaster surname, where Isabel was a prime favourite in the surname period. As Aggy (Agnes) became Taggy, so Ibby became Bibby. It seems clear that Bibby in Lancashire and Yorkshire has no connexion with the Leicestershire Beebys (v. Beebe), although some of the Beebys may now be represented by Bibby in the south of England.

headwords.meaning: the son of Bike
headwords.author_comment: The surname is a curious one, but it seems beyond dispute to have been a personal or baptismal name at the first. Amongst the New York Bicks is found 'Gustav Bick.' I find a dim. Bikelot in A. 1273. In place-names we find Bickford, Bicham, Bicknor, and Bickley, q.v., seemingly representing the personal name of the first settler.

headwords.meaning: of Bicker-dike, i.e. 'the dike of Bicker,' Bicker representing an early personal name
headwords.author_comment: I cannot find the spot. Evidently it means 'the dike of Bicker,' Bicker representing an early personal name, as is proved by such place-names as Bickerton (in cos. Chester, York, Northumberland), Bickerston (co. Norfolk), Bickering (co. Lincoln), and Bickerstaffe (co. Lancashire). Probably Lincolnshire is the home of this surname.

headwords.meaning: of Bickerstaffe, a village near Ormskirk, co. Lancashire
headwords.author_comment: In early records spelt Bikerstat and Bykyrstath. Bickersteth is found later.

headwords.meaning: of Bickerton, (1) a township in the parish of Malpas, co. Chester; (2) a township in the parish of Rothbury, co. Northumberland; (3) a township in the parish of Bilton, W. Rid. Yorks
headwords.author_comment: There can be no doubt that (3) is the chief parent, and then (1).

headwords.meaning: see Beckford
of Bikome, a West-country name (some small spot I cannot identify), with the suffix -comb; v. Bick and Combe
of Bickleigh, (1) a parish in co. Devon, four miles from Tiverton; (2) a parish in the same county, seven miles from Plymouth; (3) of Bickley, a township in the parish of Malpas, co. Chester; v. Bick
the son of Bickman, the same as the German Beckmann; v. Beckman and Bick
of Bickmore
headwords.author_comment: I cannot find the spot.

headwords.meaning: (1) of Bickenhill, a parish in co. Warwick, seven miles from Birmingham; (2) of Bickenhall, otherwise called Bicknell, a parish in co. Somerset, near Taunton; v. Bignall
of Bicknor, parishes in cos. Kent, Gloucester, and Monmouth; v. Bick
see Beadle
of Bittiscombe, a hamlet in the parish of Upton, co. Somerset, originally Biteliscombe
headwords.author_comment: The two present forms of the surname seem to be a kind of compromise.

headwords.meaning: of Biddulph, a parish in co. Stafford, three miles from Congleton
the son of Bidgood, originally Biggegod, one of a fairly large class of personal names ending in good; cf. Scattergood
headwords.author_comment: The early form is Biggegod.

headwords.meaning: the big, one of large, bulky proportions; cf. Little, Long, Short, &c.
headwords.author_comment: A familiar entry in registers of the surname epoch.

headwords.meaning: see Bickerdike
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Biggerstaff for Bickerstaff.

headwords.meaning: variant of Bickerstaff
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Biggadike for Bickerdike.

headwords.meaning: of Biggin, a township in the parish of Church Fenton, co. York; no doubt other spots are so called, from bigging, a building, biggins, buildings, i.e. a stead, a habitation, a dwelling
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Newbiggin. 'When he come to his byggynge, He welcomed fayr that lady yynge.' c. 1425: Emare, 709 (H.E.D.). 'Byggynge, or beeldynge, edificacio, structura': Prompt. Parv. p. 35.

headwords.meaning: of Bigland, an estate in the parish of Cartmell, North Lancashire
headwords.author_comment: Bigland Hall is still the residence of the Biglands.

headwords.meaning: variant of Bicknell; but Lower says 'Bignall or Bignold, a township in co. Stafford'
headwords.author_comment: But Lower says, 'Bignall or Bignold, a township in co. Stafford' (Patr. Brit p. 27). The index to the register of St. Michael, Cornhill (Harl. Soc.), refers the reader from Bicknell to Bignall. So does the Reg. Univ. Oxf. (Index, vol. ii. pt. ii).

headwords.meaning: a nickname or official term; the derisive term 'bigod', probably from the oath 'by God', later a term for religious devoteeism
headwords.author_comment: Three of these entries are of the 13th century. For the controversy on these terms, Bigod and Bigot, see Skeat's and Wedgwood's Dictionaries; also reply to Skeat by Wedgwood in the Academy, Aug. 9, 1879; see also Freeman's Norm. Conq. ii. 288. That the derisive term 'bigod' arose from the oath 'by God' seems probable. 'Pardew' (i.e. 'par Dieu') is a still existent surname with a similar origin. That it was transferred to some religious order seems equally certain (v. Wedgwood), and that through them it became a term to express religious devoteeism seems almost clear.

headwords.meaning: of Bilborough, a village parish near Tadcaster, co. York
headwords.author_comment: Bilberry seems imitative.

headwords.meaning: of Bilby, a township in the parish of Blythe, co. Notts
variant of Billcliff
the son of William
headwords.author_comment: This nick. was very uncommon; Will maintaining its hold, as Wilson, Wilkins, Wilcocks, &c., fully prove.

headwords.meaning: variant of Bellhird
of Bilcliff
headwords.author_comment: I have not identified the spot. Of course they have all one common parent; cf. bannister and baluster.

headwords.meaning: the biller, probably not a billman, i.e. one who carried a pike or halbert, but a manufacturer of the weapon
(1) of Billing, a parish in dioc. of Peterborough; (2) of Billinge, a parish in dioc. of Liverpool
headwords.author_comment: At first, no doubt, a patronymic, as proved by such place-names as Billingborough (Lincolnshire), Billingford (Norfolk), Billingham (Durham), Billinghurst, a parish in dioc. of Chichester; Billingsley, a parish in dioc. of Hereford; and Billington, a parish in dioc. of Ely.

headwords.meaning: of Billinghay, a village in co. Lincoln, about nine miles from Sleaford
of Billingham, a parish in co. Durham, near Stockton-on-Tees
of Billinghurst, a parish in co. Sussex, seven miles from Horsham
of Billingsley, a parish in co. Salop, six miles from Bridgenorth
(1) of Billington, a parish in dioc. of Ely; (2) of Billington, a township and manor in the parish of Blackburn, co. Lancashire
headwords.author_comment: The surname is well established in that county.

headwords.meaning: a bell-founder (an East-Anglian term)
headwords.author_comment: An East-Anglian term. No instances appear in the Hundred Rolls (1273). 'Belleʒetare (bellyatere), campanarius': Prompt. Parv. In the Register of Wills (London), ii. 226, occurs 'William Burford, billeytere.' I forgot to look for the date of this. Stowe informs us that Billiter Lane was once known as Belʒeters Lane. This settles the origin of the surname. 'In 1349, Thomas de Baldeswell presented to the Church aforesaid as chief lord of this fee: in 1367, Adam Humphrey: and in 1385, Adam Pyk, and in 1400, Edmund Belytter, alias Belzeter' (Blomefield's Norfolk, viii. 383).

headwords.meaning: of Bilney, a parish in co. Norfolk
headwords.author_comment: 'Thomas Bilney, or Bylney, martyr, was member of a Norfolk family which took its name from the villages of the same designation in that county': Dict. Nat. Biog. v. 40.

headwords.headword: Bilsborough, Bilsbrough, Billsborough, Bilsborow, Bilsborrow, Bilsbury, Bilsboro
headwords.meaning: of Bilsborough, a small hamlet in the parish of Garstang, co. Lancashire

headwords.meaning: the son of Bell; v. Bell (1)
headwords.author_comment: There is no evidence in favour of 'the son of Bill,' i.e. William. That nick. is comparatively modern. In the Modern Domesday Book (co. Warwick) there are four Bellisons, one Belson, and one Bilson, all evidently of the same stock, namely, Bellson (i.e. the son of Isabella). Bilson is an easy variant of Belson.

headwords.meaning: of Bilton, a village parish about nine miles west of York
a corruption of Binson, itself a corrupted form of Benson
the book-binder
headwords.author_comment: This is practically settled by the Hundred Rolls, where, in the town of Oxford, Stephen Ligator, librorum, is mentioned again as Stephen Ligator. Also in the case of a William Ligator, as below; v. Bookbinder.

headwords.meaning: of Bindlows; the suffix is -low (v. Lowe)
headwords.author_comment: I cannot find the spot. It is clear that the suffix is -low (v. Lowe).

headwords.meaning: of Bingham, a parish in dioc. of Southwell, co. Nottingham
of Bingley, a parish and market town in the West Rid. Yorks
headwords.modern_distribution: West Riding Court Dir., 14; London, 10; Philadelphia, 4

of Binnie, an estate in the parish of Uphall, Linlithgowshire (Lower's Patr. Brit. p. 28)
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 1, 3; West Riding Court Dir., 4, 0; Boston (U.S.), 16, 0

headwords.meaning: the son of Binning; v. Benning, and cf. Browning and Harding

Welsh, Ap-Ennion; v. Bennion and Benyon
(?) local
headwords.author_comment: This surname has ramified most strongly in co. York.
