headwords.meaning: variant of Birkbeck
at the birch, from residence by a birch-tree (cf. Oak, Ash, Nash, &c.); v. Birks
headwords.author_comment: In Lancashire, Birch generally hails from Birch, a chapelry in the parish of Middleton, near Manchester. Of course, a surname of this class is originated in a hundred different places. Every directory teems with the name.

headwords.meaning: of Birtles; v. Birtles
headwords.author_comment: Odd as this may seem, it is true. For further evidence, v. Birtles.

headwords.meaning: of the birchen-hough, from residence thereby; the mound or hill covered with birches
headwords.author_comment: Birchen is the adjective of birch, a birch-tree or trees (cf. Golden), and hough, like haugh, or how, means a hill or mound. Hence Birchenhough is simply the mound or hill covered with birches; cf. Goodenough. In both cases the h is elided.

headwords.meaning: at the birchwood, from residence by a clump or grove of birch-trees
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Birkinshaw, an exact equivalent.

headwords.meaning: variant of Birkinshaw
the bird, perhaps from the singing propensities of the original bearer
headwords.author_comment: Cf. 'He sings like a bird.' Also cf. Nightingale, Sparrow, Finch, Lark, &c.

headwords.meaning: (?) of Birstall, a village parish near Dewsbury, Yorks
headwords.modern_distribution: Church Fenton (Yorks), 1, 0, 0; West Riding Court Dir., 0, 2, 0; Sheffield, 0, 0, 1; Philadelphia, 3, 0, 0

headwords.meaning: of Birdsey; the meaning seems clear, the 'Birdseye,' i.e. the islet or eyot in the stream frequented by birds
headwords.author_comment: I cannot find the spot. Manifestly Birdseye is imitative. The index under 'Birdsey' refers the reader to 'Budsey.'
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 3, 1; MDB. (co. Bedford), 0, 2; New York, 4, 0; Philadelphia, 1, 0

headwords.meaning: a somewhat pretty imitative corruption of Birtwhistle, q.v.
of Birkbeck, so called from the beck or streamlet that flowed through the birks or birch-trees (v. Birks and Beck)
headwords.author_comment: A Cumberland surname. Of course, Birkbeck was too big a mouthful for ordinary and current usage, and Birbeck took its place.

headwords.meaning: of Birkenhead, co. Chester; the head of the birch-trees
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Aikenhead, and v. Birkett and Birkhead.

headwords.meaning: North English, of the birk-head, i.e. the head of the birches; cf. Birkenhead and Beckett
headwords.author_comment: The surname Haslefoot is of the same class.

headwords.meaning: of Birkenshaw, a chapelry in the parish of Birstall, co. York; 'the birch-wood,' birken being the adjective (v. Birkenhead, Akenhead, &c.)
headwords.author_comment: The variants are curious, but only found at a distance from their native home. The Standard of Oct. 12, 1886, p. 3, reports Emma Bircumshaw as appearing in court at Nottingham in a legal case. This spelling is a manifest corruption of Birkinshaw.
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 1, 0, 3, 0, 0; MDB. (West Rid. Yorks), 2, 5, 0, 0, 0; (co. Notts), 0, 0, 0, 0, 2; Manchester, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0

headwords.meaning: at the birks, from residence beside a clump of birch-trees; North English birk, a birch-tree
headwords.author_comment: V. Birkenhead, Birkett, Birkbeck, &c.; and v. Birch.

headwords.meaning: of Birley or Burley, several places in co. York; v. Burley and Burleigh
of Birtles, a township in the parish of Prestbury, co. Cheshire, formerly spelt Birchels as well as Birtles; v. Birchall
of Birtwistle
headwords.author_comment: I cannot find the spot; cf. Entwistle. But as it is evidently in the West Rid. Yorks, it may be an early form of Briestwhistle, a hamlet in the parish of Thornhill. Birdwhistle (q.v.) is a curious imitative form. The fact that Anthony was at Brasenose College is all but absolute proof that he came from co. Lanc.
headwords.modern_distribution: Manchester, 1, 4; MDB. (co. York, West Rid.), 2, 1; Philadelphia, 0, 2

headwords.meaning: the bishop; a sobriquet readily affixed on one of ecclesiastical appearance; most Bishops owe their title to the custom of electing a boy-bishop on St. Nicholas' Day
headwords.author_comment: A common entry in early registers, a sobriquet readily affixed on one of ecclesiastical appearance. Nevertheless, most of our Bishops owe their title to the custom of electing a boy-bishop on St. Nicholas' Day (v. Brand, Pop. Antiq.). The ceremony was a very familiar one. Lyson quotes from the Lambeth Churchwardens' Accounts, 1523: 'For the Bishop's dynner and hys company on St. Nycolas' Day, iis. viiid.' King arose similarly, q.v. A curious proof of the existence of this popular nickname is seen in the following entry: Bissop atte Comb. In the formal roll of the Preston Guild Merchant for 1602 appears the name of 'William Browne, alias Bushopp' (Preston Guild Rolls, p. 64).

headwords.meaning: (?) probably the suffix is -rigg, a ridge
of Bispham, a village three miles from Poulton, in the Fylde district, co. Lancashire; anciently Biscopham, i.e. the bishop's dwelling (v. Baines' Hist. Lanc. ii. 507)
variant of Bysh
the son of Biset
headwords.author_comment: This so far tallies with Mr. Ferguson's statement that Bissett is a dim. of an old Teutonic personal name Bis. But I suspect that Biset is the full name, and not a diminutive (v. Lower's Patr. Brit. p. 29).
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0; MDB. (W. Rid. Yorks), 0, 0, 2, 0, 0; West Rid. Court Dir., 2, 0, 0, 1, 0; Philadelphia, 11, 0, 0, 0, 2

headwords.meaning: a tell-tale; M.E. blabbe, a tell-tale
headwords.author_comment: Simon le Blabe (Close Roll, 3 Edw. I); M.E. blabbe, a tell-tale. 'Blabbe, or labbe, wreyare of cownselle': Prompt. Parv.

headwords.meaning: the blabber, a revealer of secrets, a tell-tale; v. Blab
headwords.author_comment: '1557. He was a great blabber of his tongue' (H.E.D.).

headwords.meaning: of Blaby, a parish in dioc. of Peterborough and co. Leicester
the black, from the complexion
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Blackman, Blue, White, Hoare, Blunt, Russell, &c.

headwords.meaning: of Blackadder, not far from the English border in Scotland
headwords.author_comment: A river of that name also runs there.

headwords.meaning: of the Black-hall
headwords.author_comment: Mr. Lower says that it is a corruption of Blackwell, but this is not borne out by evidence.

headwords.meaning: v. Ballock (H.E.D.)
with the black beard; M.E. berd or berde
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Brownbeard. Blackbird is an imitative form. Blackberd occurs in Yorkshire so early as 1379. It is still to be met with there in the shape of Blackbeard.

headwords.meaning: of Blackburn, a large and thriving town in co. Lanc.
headwords.author_comment: There is no negro taint in Blackborn.

headwords.meaning: of Blackhall, co. Lanc.; from Black-hall, near Preston, pronounced Blackow
headwords.author_comment: This looks like a nickname or sign-board name, but it is from Black-hall, near Preston; pronounced Blackow (cf. Lindow for Lindale, Picthaw for Pickthall, &c). This name has taken the imitative form of Blackcow: William Blackcow (Proctor's Manchester Streets). In this same series of records the surname is variously spelled Blacoll, Blacoe, Blackowe, Blakecowe, and Blakow; v. Index.

headwords.meaning: (1) the son of Blacre (Domesday); (2) the bleacher; for a feminine form, v. Blaxter
(1) at the Blackhead, the dark headland, from residence thereby; cf. Birket and Becket, for Birkhead and Beckhead (v. Redhead); (2) with the black head; cf. Whitehead
headwords.author_comment: In any case the original form is Blackhead.
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 8, 0; MDB. (co. Northumberland), 3, 1; New York, 1, 0; Boston (U.S.), 1, 0

headwords.meaning: (?) with the black or very dark eyes; but it may be local
headwords.author_comment: But it may be local; v. my first instance and cf. Birdseye.

headwords.meaning: of Blackford, (1) a parish in co. Soms., near Wincanton; (2) a chapelry in the parish of Wedmore, co. Soms., near Axbridge
variant of Blackall
of Blakenham; probably the same as Blakenham: two parishes, Great and Little Blakenham, near Ipswich
headwords.author_comment: My instances all point to this.

headwords.meaning: the bleacher; v. Blaxter
the black lamb, the naughty, the bad
headwords.author_comment: William Blacklambe (Close Roll, 8 Edw. III). Cf. 'Ba, ba, blacksheep, have you any wool?' also 'black sheep,' for a man of exceptionally bad qualities.

headwords.meaning: of the Black-lake, corrupted by imitation into Blackleach
headwords.author_comment: Probably the spot mentioned in a charter (c. 1200) connected with property in Wilmslow parish, East Cheshire, from which district the name in most cases is undoubtedly sprung. 'Fulseha, Chorlegh, Pounale, and Morlegh, . . . as far as the mid stream of the Siche, which comes from the Black Lache of Shadoke mosse,' &c. Mr. Earwaker adds, 'The name Black Lache or Black Lake is now applied to a large pond on Lindow Common' (East Ches. i. 42); v. Depledge and Cartledge.

headwords.meaning: the bachelor
headwords.author_comment: A surname peculiar to the West country, especially to co. Devon. The two instances below pave the way to the little eccentricity of Blackler; v. Batchelar.

headwords.headword: Blackley, Blakeley, Bleackley, Bleckly, Blakely, Bleakley
headwords.meaning: (1) of Blackley (usually pronounced Blakeley), a township in the old parish of Manchester; (2) of Blakeney, q.v.
headwords.author_comment: This corruption was an early one; v. infra, and cf. Blankley for Blankney.

headwords.meaning: with the black lock of hair (cf. Silverlock, Goldlock, Lovelock)
headwords.author_comment: A familiar Cumberland surname.

headwords.meaning: the blackman, i.e. the dark-complexioned man
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Black and Blacklock, White, Whiteman, and Whitman.

headwords.meaning: of Blanchminster; Latinized into 'De Albo Monasterio'
headwords.author_comment: Killminster and Killmaster (q.v.) seem quite as repellent, and have a similar origin. Black = O.E. blāc, white, pale. Lower gives the name as now existing. I have not met with it.

headwords.meaning: of Blackmore: (1) Blackmoor, parish in dioc. of Winchester; (2) Blackmore, parish in dioc. of St. Albans
headwords.author_comment: The form Blakamour seems to suggest a French nickname; cf. Phillimore, Parramore, &c. Still, it is better to consider the a as intrusive, as in Greenaway, Ottaway, Hathaway, &c.

headwords.meaning: variant of Blakesley
a worker in iron
headwords.author_comment: This and Whitesmith are the only survivals of the custom of styling the different workers in metals by the colour of that on which they spent their energies; cf. Whitesmith, Greensmith, Redsmith, Brownsmith. 'Brydel-bytters, blackesmythes, and ferrars': Cocke Lorelle's Bote.

headwords.meaning: (Personal) the son of Black; cf. Brownson or Greenson
headwords.author_comment: Sometimes, no doubt, a corruption of Blackstone, a local surname. But the above derivation is in general the correct one, baptismal or personal names from colours not being uncommon.

headwords.meaning: of Blaxton, a township in the parish of Finningley, West Rid. Yorks.; no doubt originally Blackston or Blackstone
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Buxton for Buckstone. Of William Blackstone, one of the earliest episcopal clergymen resident in New England (d. 1675), a biographer writes: 'His name was variantly spelled Blackstone, Blackston, and Blaxton': Dict. Nat. Biog. v. 132. But it is not likely that Blaxton in co. York is the sole parent of Blackstone and its variants. Doubtless other places in South England of the same name have had their share in making up the list of surnames found in our modern directories.

headwords.meaning: (1) of Blackwell, a parish in co. Derby near Alfreton; (2) of Blackwell, a township in the parish of Darlington, co. Durham
headwords.author_comment: Other and smaller places could also be cited.

headwords.meaning: (?) the son of Blade
headwords.author_comment: An unquestionable compound personal name occurs in the case of Gilbert Bladewine, co. Norf., 1273. A; cf. Unwin, Goodwin, &c.

headwords.meaning: the blade-smith, a sword manufacurer
headwords.author_comment: The 'Cuttellers, Bladesmythes, and Shethers' went together in the York Pageant (York Mystery Plays, p. xxiii, ed. Toulmin Smith). Cocke Lorelle's Bote couples 'cutlers and bladesmythes.' 'Bladsmythe, scindifaber': Prompt. Parv.

headwords.meaning: of Bladon, a parish in Oxfordshire, near Woodstock
variant of Blakebrough
of Blagdon: (1) a township in the parish of Stannington, co. Northumberland; (2) a parish in co. Somerset, eight miles from Axbridge
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Slagg and Slack.

headwords.meaning: (?) the black (?), from the dark hair or swarthy complexion of the nominee; a variant of Black
headwords.author_comment: A variant of Black, q.v.; cf. Slagg and Slack, Higgs and Hicks. Even Jack is found as Jagge in Piers Plowman's Vision; cf. Blagrove for Blackgrove, or Blamire for Blackmire.

headwords.meaning: of Blagrave, a tithing in the parish of Lambourn, co. Berks; lit. 'the black grove'

headwords.meaning: variant of Blackmore

of Blakesley, a parish in co. Northampton, four miles from Towcester
headwords.author_comment: Blacksley is a modern variant.

headwords.meaning: the blamer, with fem. suffix -ster
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Brewster, Spinster, &c.

headwords.meaning: of the blamire, i.e. black mire, from residence thereby
headwords.author_comment: A North-country name; v. Myers.

headwords.meaning: the son of Blanche
headwords.author_comment: Sometimes, no doubt, a nickname answering to English 'White.'

headwords.meaning: 'Blanchard,' O.F. blanchart, whitish; a sobriquet of complexion
headwords.author_comment: Probably used as a fontal name. It was used as the name for a white horse; cf. Bayard, for a bay horse. 'Vppon my stede blanchard thu ridest here.' c. 1440, Generydes (H.E.D.). [Of the form Blanket:] This last form is imitative, and still lives.

headwords.meaning: the son of Blanchefleur, Angl. 'white-flower'
headwords.author_comment: There is the story of 'Floriz and Blancheflour,' E. E. Text Society (circa 1280). Lower sets down the corrupted Branchflower as still existing. From Somersetshire the surname seems to have travelled into Devonshire.

headwords.meaning: of Blanchfront, from some spot in Normandy
headwords.author_comment: Not a nickname, as suggested by Lower.

headwords.meaning: 'white hand,' q.v.
headwords.author_comment: Lower says, 'Fr. blanches mains, "white hands." From this peculiarity Robert de Beaumont, 3rd Earl of Leicester, received his sobriquet. It also became the hereditary surname of a family' (Patr. Brit. p. 30).

headwords.meaning: of Blancpain, some spot in Normandy, of which the English translation was Whitebread and Whitbread, q.v.
headwords.author_comment: Blanchpain has a strong nickname appearance about it, but the evidence is against such a derivation. Eugene Aram was usher, in 1744, to the Rev. Mr. Painblanc, in Piccadilly.

headwords.meaning: of Bland, one of the four hamlets of which the town of Sedburgh (co. York) is comprised
headwords.author_comment: It is not a complimentary nickname, but distinctly local. The name ramified strongly.

the bleacher, with fem. suffix -ster
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Baxter. 'Pleykstare, candidarius'; 'whytstare or pleykstare, candidarius, candidaria'; 'bleystare or wytstare (bleykester, or whytster), candidarius' (Prompt. Parv.). Robert Blaxter appeared as defendant in a Norfolk case at the close of the 16th century (Proceedings in Chancery, Elizabeth, i. 250). Both Blaxter and Blackistor still exist. For masculine form, v. Blacker (2).

headwords.headword: Blaze, Blazey, Blazy, Blease, Bleas, Blase
headwords.meaning: the son of Blaze
headwords.author_comment: St. Blaise was the patron saint of wool-combers, and his festival (Feb. 3) till recent days was faithfully commemorated in Yorkshire. A full-sized effigy of the bishop is carved in the principal entrance to the Bradford Exchange. As a font-name Blaise, or Blaze, just managed to survive the Reformation. Gil Blas has immortalized the name in literature; v. Puritan Nomenclature, pp. 93, 94.

headwords.meaning: of Bleasdale, a chapelry in the parish of Lancaster
headwords.author_comment: The surname is still chiefly found in that district. But it has managed to cross the Atlantic, and lives in Boston in a slightly varied form.
